95% confidence intervals in brackets, transformed from the coefficient interval.

Read one coefficient for each cohort and post-adoption date. At adoption, cohort 2 has 18.5% higher expected visits in the pooled fit. The interval below the estimate is a pointwise 95% interval based on unit clustering. The fixed-effect rows list absorbed blocks. The pooled fit includes cohort and period indicators as ordinary regressors.

The two PPML columns agree here in a balanced, no-covariate panel, as in Wooldridge’s comparison in §3.3. Adding covariates or changing support can break this agreement. Wooldridge’s Proposition 3.1 establishes a different equivalence, between pooled canonical-link QMLE and the imputation procedure under its conditions. Its Poisson argument does not carry over to a Gamma score with a log link. The cancelled Gamma column differs because the four-period histories yield different weights. Both cancelled fits can recover unit effects with fixef() and return fitted expected visits with predict(). To switch off the policy, set the cohort-period treatment indicators to zero on the retained rows and pass those rows to predict(). This holds the recovered effects fixed. The DiD aggregation and inference example below builds its own table from a pooled PPML fit. Prediction and counterfactuals

Plot the cohort-by-period effects

This Matplotlib figure uses the pooled PPML percentages and pointwise intervals for the same five cells shown in the table.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

effects = pooled.effects(list(CELLS.values())).set_index("term")
points = 100 * effects["estimate"]
lower = 100 * effects["conf_low"]
upper = 100 * effects["conf_high"]
labels = [cell_labels[term] for term in effects.index]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 3.6), layout="constrained")
ax.errorbar(points, labels, xerr=[points - lower, upper - points],
            fmt="o", color="#215873", capsize=4)
ax.axvline(0, color="0.45", linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set(xlabel="Change in expected visits (%)", title="Cohort-by-period effects with 95% intervals")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("did-cohort-effects.png", dpi=175)

Adjust for a time-varying covariate

Suppose service visits also depend on an exogenous, time-varying covariate x. The script draws a different path for each unit, independently of its baseline, adoption and outcome shocks. A one-unit increase in x multiplies its untreated mean by exp⁡(0.35)\exp(0.35). The policy multipliers and the 15% common period growth at fixed x are the same as above. In an application, use a pretreatment covariate or one that treatment cannot affect. Conditional multiplicative parallel trends require the same untreated growth across cohorts at a common covariate path. The design also requires no anticipation and untreated comparisons with overlapping covariate support at the relevant dates. Identification assumptions

For two periods, fit visits ~ 0 + treated + x | unit + period. The example script fits each working variance on the same panel, checks the exact retained row positions, and reports 100(exp⁡(β̂)−1)100(\exp(\hat\beta)-1) for each treatment indicator. In both comparisons, the number in parentheses below each estimate is its unit-clustered standard error in percentage points.

import numpy as np

def comparison_rows(fits, panel, terms):
    """Display each percentage effect above its unit-clustered SE."""
    first = next(iter(fits.values()))
    for fit in fits.values():
        np.testing.assert_array_equal(fit.sample.positions, first.sample.positions)
        assert fit.sample.labels.equals(panel.iloc[fit.sample.positions].index)
    table = pm.etable(
        *fits.values(), names=tuple(fits), keep=terms, scale="effect",
        uncertainty="se", stars=False, digits=2,
    )
    # Each requested term occupies two rows before the model statistics.
    rows = table.to_frame(formatted=True).head(2 * len(terms))
    return rows.rename(columns={"": "term"})[["term", *fits]]

two_period = did_data(with_x=True)
methods = {"Joint PPML": (1, None), "Cancelled 1.5": (1.5, "unit"),
           "Cancelled Gamma": (2, "unit")}
two_fits = {
    name: pm.fit("visits ~ 0 + treated + x | unit + period", two_period,
                 omega=1, tau=tau, cancel=cancel, cluster="unit")
    for name, (tau, cancel) in methods.items()
}
print(f"Two periods with X: {two_fits['Joint PPML'].sample.count} retained rows")
print(comparison_rows(two_fits, two_period, ["treated"]).to_string(index=False))

treated      31.62         31.76           31.81
           (16.46)       (16.45)         (16.44)

Two units had zero visits in both periods. All three fits used the same 158 remaining units. Once x changes differently across units within a cohort, the cancelled estimating functions can give those units different relative weights. The three point estimates are close in this draw.

For staggered adoption, include x alongside the five treatment indicators. Pooled PPML includes cohort and period indicators. The other three fits use unit and period effects. All four fits cluster by unit. For example, g2_t3 compares treatment with no treatment for cohort 2 in period 3.

staggered = did_data(staggered=True, with_x=True)
adjusted_formula = f"visits ~ 1 + C(cohort) + C(period) + {rhs} + x"
adjusted = pm.fit(adjusted_formula, staggered, omega=1, tau=1, cluster="unit")
fits_x = {"Pooled PPML": adjusted}
for name, (tau, cancel) in methods.items():
    fits_x[name] = pm.fit(f"visits ~ 0 + {rhs} + x | unit + period", staggered,
                         omega=1, tau=tau, cancel=cancel, cluster="unit")
print(f"Staggered with X: {adjusted.sample.count} retained rows")
print(comparison_rows(fits_x, staggered, list(CELLS.values())).to_string(index=False))

What the reported effects measure

Overall effect on visits. The pooled PPML fit predicts 6.520 visits per treated unit-period under the observed policy and 4.850 without it. The comparison covers 400 treated observations from 160 units.

Both tables use the full covariance matrix from the fit, clustered by unit across all 240 units. The SEs and pointwise 95% normal intervals hold the observed treated rows, their covariates and their weights fixed. Weighting the cell ATTs by their treated-row counts reproduces the overall ATT. Its SE includes the covariance between cells. Covariance conventions

Reproduce the overall ATT and its SE

Select the exact retained treated rows. Predict visits once under the observed policy and again with only the five adoption-cell indicators set to zero. Cohort, period and x are identical in both predictions.

retained = staggered.iloc[adjusted.sample.positions]
assert retained.index.equals(adjusted.sample.labels)
treated = retained.loc[retained["treated"] == 1]
no_policy = treated.copy()
no_policy[list(CELLS.values())] = 0
observed = adjusted.predict(treated)
untreated = adjusted.predict(no_policy)
assert observed.index.equals(treated.index) and untreated.index.equals(treated.index)
att = (observed - untreated).mean()
ratio = observed.sum() / untreated.sum()

For an exponential mean, a prediction’s derivative with respect to the coefficients is its fitted value times its design row. Average the observed and no-policy derivatives over the same rows. Their difference is the gradient of the level ATT. For the percentage increase, apply the quotient rule. Keep the fitted coefficient order in both gradients and the covariance.

from formulaic import model_matrix

names = adjusted.coef().index
design = model_matrix(adjusted_formula.split("~", 1)[1], retained).model_spec
x1 = design.get_model_matrix(treated).loc[:, names].to_numpy()
x0 = design.get_model_matrix(no_policy).loc[:, names].to_numpy()
d1 = (observed.to_numpy()[:, None] * x1).mean(axis=0)
d0 = (untreated.to_numpy()[:, None] * x0).mean(axis=0)
gradient = d1 - d0
vcov = adjusted.vcov().loc[names, names].to_numpy()
se_att = np.sqrt(gradient @ vcov @ gradient)
gradient_pct = 100 * (d1 - ratio * d0) / untreated.mean()
se_pct = np.sqrt(gradient_pct @ vcov @ gradient_pct)

The example script uses the same calculation for each cohort-period row, averaging the derivatives within that cell. Runnable example

Relate the specification to Stata jwdid

In jwdid, the cohort variable records the first period treated and zero for never-treated units. Its default cohort-by-time effects allow different effects by cohort and calendar date. The following are corresponding Stata specifications for a panel with these column names.

jwdid visits, ivar(unit) tvar(period) gvar(cohort) method(poisson)
estat simple
estat event

jwdid visits, ivar(unit) tvar(period) gvar(cohort) method(ppmlhdfe)

method(poisson) uses cohort and period indicators for pooled Poisson regression. With ivar(unit), method(ppmlhdfe) estimates Poisson with unit and period effects. estat simple averages fitted treatment-versus-no treatment differences among treated observations. estat event groups them by time since adoption. With never, the comparison uses the never-treated group and the command also allows pre-treatment deviations relative to the reference period. This changes the specification and the comparison group. Pre-period checks can reveal discrepancies but cannot establish the counterfactual post-treatment trend.

Match controls, support, reference periods, clustering and aggregation weights when comparing software. Powermean produced the tables above. The Stata syntax follows the command documentation and source. jwdid nonlinear estimation and postestimation · jwdid source

Estimate a trade agreement slope in a gravity model

How much more do two countries trade in years when they have an agreement? The example follows pairs of countries over time, including years with zero trade. It compares the same pair with and without an agreement while accounting for conditions in each country and year. The model for expected trade is

E[Yijt∣X,α,γ,δ]=exp⁡(βDijt+αij+γit+δjt). E[Y_{ijt}\mid X,\alpha,\gamma,\delta] =\exp(\beta D_{ijt}+\alpha_{ij}+\gamma_{it}+\delta_{jt}).

Here DijtD_{ijt} is the agreement indicator, XX contains the panel regressors, and the three fixed-effect terms represent a directed pair, an exporter-year and an importer-year. The target is the conditional arithmetic mean of trade. For a change in DD from zero to one with the fixed effects held constant, the model gives the ratio exp⁡(β)\exp(\beta).

Create the trade panel

After installing Powermean, run the following in a Python session. It generates all the data used below. The same example is also available as a standalone script.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import powermean as pm

rng = np.random.default_rng(20261118)
countries = range(12)
years = np.arange(8)
exporter, importer = np.array(
    [(i, j) for i in countries for j in countries if i != j]
).T
n_pairs = len(exporter)

adoption_year = rng.integers(1, 12, size=n_pairs)
agreement = years[None, :] >= adoption_year[:, None]
pair_effect = rng.normal(0, 0.35, size=(n_pairs, 1))
exporter_year = rng.normal(0, 0.25, size=(len(countries), len(years)))
importer_year = rng.normal(0, 0.25, size=(len(countries), len(years)))
mean = np.exp(
    1.2 + pair_effect + exporter_year[exporter] + importer_year[importer]
    + 0.35 * agreement
)

trade = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "exporter": np.repeat(exporter, len(years)),
        "importer": np.repeat(importer, len(years)),
        "year": np.tile(2001 + years, n_pairs),
        "pair": np.repeat(np.arange(n_pairs), len(years)),
        "agreement": agreement.astype(int).ravel(),
        "trade": rng.poisson(mean).ravel(),
    }
)
print(pm.summary_statistics(trade, vars=("trade",), probs=(0, 0.5, 1)))
Summary statistics                                      N = 1,056 rows
----------------------------------------------------------------------
           N  missing  mean    sd    p0   p50   p100  zeros  mean | >0
----------------------------------------------------------------------
trade  1,056        0  4.08  3.25  0.00  3.00  37.00   6.0%       4.33
----------------------------------------------------------------------

The simulation has 12 countries, all 132 directed foreign pairs, and eight years for each pair. There is no domestic trade in this design. Agreements start at different dates, with some pairs untreated throughout. Adoption dates are drawn independently by directed pair for this exercise. Real agreements are often reciprocal, in which case the appropriate clustering may differ. Trade is drawn in levels from a Poisson distribution with pair-specific baselines, country-year shifts and an agreement slope of 0.35. This makes the examples reproducible and shows how to handle genuine zeros.

Fit with three fixed-effect blocks

formula = "trade ~ 0 + agreement | pair + exporter^year + importer^year"
fit = pm.fit(
    formula, trade, omega=1, tau=1, cancel=None, bias_correction=False,
    vcov={"cluster": "pair"},
)
print(fit.summary())
powermean

Fixed-effect block counts (fitted rows, active covariance)

Nested blocks count as fully redundant in these block counts.

The console summary shows the estimator, the three jointly estimated blocks, the number of usable observations and the numerical status. The agreement row is on the log mean scale.

  • omega=1 models the arithmetic mean. tau=1 specifies the power working variance V(m)=mV(m)=m and gives PPML. The PPML moment needs a correctly specified mean for its usual interpretation. Its use extends to nonnegative outcomes measured in continuous units.
  • Terms after | are fixed-effect blocks. pair identifies a directed exporter–importer pair. ^ creates one interaction block per term. 0 + omits a separate intercept because the effect indicators already span a constant. The fit estimates the blocks jointly through absorption.
  • The covariance sums score contributions within each of the 132 pairs before combining them. That matches independent pair histories and allows arbitrary dependence within a history under the pair-sandwich assumptions. Shared shocks across pairs require a separate sampling argument.

All 63 zero flows contribute to the fit. In other data, some patterns of zeros can imply separation and change the estimation sample. Inspect fit.sample and fit.summary() for the actual sample and diagnostics. Prepare your data

Identify the slope

Pair effects absorb permanent bilateral differences such as distance. Exporter-year effects absorb shifts common to all partners of an exporter in a year, and importer-year effects do the analogous job for importers. The agreement slope uses within-pair changes in policy that remain after both country-year blocks are accounted for. A policy that moves identically for all destinations of an exporter in each year would be absorbed by the exporter-year block, even if it changes within pairs.

These controls identify a coefficient of the maintained mean model when enough variation remains. A causal trade-policy interpretation in an observational panel also needs assumptions about policy timing and other time-varying bilateral shocks. The model holds exporter-year and importer-year effects fixed when computing this comparison. A counterfactual in which those effects respond to policy requires an additional model.

The outcome table reports 45.5% more average trade in observed agreement years. That comparison uses the two observed groups of rows. The regression’s 53.9% holds the three fixed-effect blocks constant. Read the two numbers as answers to their respective comparisons. Both tables use the same simulated panel and were reproduced with Powermean 0.1.1. Benatia et al. (2026), §§2–3 and 5 · Weidner and Zylkin (2021), §§3.1–3.4

Continue with the same model

Read fixed effects to compare joint absorption with pair cancellation on this panel. Read coefficient bias and covariance refinements to see how the adjustments in Weidner and Zylkin (2021) change the agreement estimate and its interval.

Difference out two fixed-effect blocks

GMM1 and GMM2 estimate slopes in an exponential mean model with two fixed effects. Both compare outcomes in groups of four observations, so neither fixed effect enters the slope equation. Use these estimators for a complete panel, such as firms observed in every year, or a complete set of directed links, such as trade between countries. Jochmans (2017), §§I–III · Open manuscript

When is the comparison valid?

Take two firms i,ki,k observed in two years j,ℓj,\ell. Write μij=aigjexp⁡(xij′β)\mu_{ij}=a_i g_j\exp(x_{ij}'\beta) for expected output and Uij=Yij/μijU_{ij}=Y_{ij}/\mu_{ij} for the multiplicative error. Let CC denote the full regressor array and both sets of fixed effects. The mean model gives E[Uij∣C]=1E[U_{ij}\mid C]=1 for each observation.

GMM1 and GMM2 also compare the products on the two diagonals. For this comparison to average to zero at the true slope, the rectangle must satisfy

E[UijUkℓ∣C]=E[UiℓUkj∣C]. E[U_{ij}U_{k\ell}\mid C]=E[U_{i\ell}U_{kj}\mid C].

This is an extra assumption. A shock shared by the two observations on one diagonal can preserve each conditional mean and still change their expected product. Jochmans (2017) derives the moment with both conditional products equal to one. The reported standard errors use the paper’s cell-based variance calculation under conditional independence across observations and large-array regularity conditions. In a panel, both the number of firms and the number of years must grow for this inference. Jochmans (2017), eqs. (1.3)–(1.4) and Theorem 2

Choose the observed array

Pass one row per observed cell, with finite regressors and a finite, nonnegative outcome. Put the two identifiers after | and omit the intercept with 0 +. Set estimator="gmm1" or estimator="gmm2" to choose the moment equation.

Rectangular panels

Use fe_layout="rectangular" (the default for GMM fits, corresponding to twexp) for a complete crossing with at least two levels on each axis. A panel needs one row per unit and period. The unit and period labels are separate, and the two dimensions can have different lengths. A two-by-two panel contains only one rectangle, so it cannot yield usable cell-projection standard errors. The fit refuses with unusable_covariance if it reaches a root on that layout.

The twexp help illustrates the method with firms’ patent counts and log R&D spending, originally stored in separate columns for each year. Reshape such data to long format before fitting. To follow the authors’ example of using the GMM1 slopes to initialize GMM2, keep the formula and its column order fixed.

import powermean as pm

formula = "patents ~ 0 + log_rd | firm + year"
gmm1 = pm.fit(formula, firm_year, estimator="gmm1")
gmm2 = pm.fit(formula, firm_year, estimator="gmm2", start=gmm1.coef())
print(pm.etable(gmm1, gmm2, uncertainty="ci"))

Directed dyads

Use fe_layout="directed" (corresponding to twgravity) for a cross-section of ordered pairs of agents. Supply every ordered non-self link among at least four agents. Use the same labels for an agent in the origin and destination columns. The outcome and regressors may differ in opposite directions.

The twgravity help fits trade flows in levels using bilateral variables such as log distance, a shared border and a shared language.

fit = pm.fit(
    "trade ~ 0 + log_distance + border + common_language | exporter + importer",
    bilateral_trade, estimator="gmm2", fe_layout="directed",
)
print(fit.summary())

An observed zero stays in the sample. Missing pairs, duplicate pairs, missing or non-finite model values, and self-links in the directed layout raise SampleError. To restrict the fit as you would with Stata’s if or in, filter the data frame first and pass a complete array on the selected levels. Runnable examples for both layouts

Choose the moment equation

Write p=xij+xkℓp=x_{ij}+x_{k\ell}, q=xiℓ+xkjq=x_{i\ell}+x_{kj}, P=yijykℓP=y_{ij}y_{k\ell} and Q=yiℓykjQ=y_{i\ell}y_{kj}. Both methods set the average of (p−q)D(b)(p-q)D(b) to zero over admissible rectangles. Directed rectangles use four distinct agent labels.

Method Difference D(b)D(b)
"gmm1" Pexp⁡(−p′b)−Qexp⁡(−q′b)P\exp(-p'b)-Q\exp(-q'b)
"gmm2" Pexp⁡(q′b)−Qexp⁡(p′b)P\exp(q'b)-Q\exp(p'b)

GMM2 multiplies each GMM1 rectangle by exp⁡((p+q)′b)\exp((p+q)'b). Both target the same identified slope under the rectangle restriction, but rectangles receive different weights and the estimates can differ in a given sample.

PML also offers a choice of weights, applied to a different quantity. At omega=1, a PML score with working variance μτ\mu^\tau weights each observation’s relative residual Y/μ−1Y/\mu-1 by μ2−τ\mu^{2-\tau}. PPML gives more weight to observations with larger means. Gamma PML weights relative residuals equally. Changing tau reweights these single-observation residuals. Choosing between GMM1 and GMM2 reweights four-observation contrasts, and both choices require the extra product restriction above. Mean and working variance · Benatia et al. (2026), §3.2

Each GMM equation has one moment per slope. The Newton solver starts at zero unless you pass a finite vector in coefficient order with start=. Use max_iter= to set the iteration limit.

An intercept, an additive row or column regressor, or dependent rectangle contrasts raise IdentificationError. The solver also requires a resolved full-rank Jacobian at the evaluated point. Both a scaled moment and a local Newton correction must pass before inference. The returned fit.certificate.status is "local_solution"; existence and outcome can depend on the data and the start. Troubleshoot a refusal

Read uncertainty and compare with Stata

Use fit.coef(), fit.se(), fit.vcov(), fit.confint(), fit.tidy() and fit.summary(). fit.sample.positions and fit.sample.retained_index keep input order. pm.etable can display fitted slopes or their unit-change transformations exp(b) - 1.

Each projection row sums the kernels of rectangles incident on that observed cell. With MM rectangles and NN observed cells, the projection is hs=(N/M)∑r∋s(pr−qr)Dr(b)h_s=(N/M)\sum_{r\ni s}(p_r-q_r)D_r(b). Let GG be the derivative of the mean moment. The vcov="paper" default uses G−1(∑shshs′/N)G−𝖳/NG^{-1}(\sum_s h_s h_s'/N)G^{-\mathsf T}/N and normal-reference intervals. In the rectangle M=(I2)(J2)M=\binom{I}{2}\binom{J}{2} and N=IJN=IJ. In the directed array M=(n2)(n−22)M=\binom{n}{2}\binom{n-2}{2} and N=n(n−1)N=n(n-1).

Use vcov="stata" to apply the twgravity additional multiplier (n−1)/n(n-1)/n for directed fits. The source averages projection products over its n2n^2 matrix slots and uses the observed NN for the final coefficient covariance. The option has unit multiplier in the rectangle. fit.with_vcov("stata") changes the reporting convention on an existing fit. Both layouts use cell projections as their available inference.

Powermean subtracts the mean of the observed design columns before solving. In the source comparisons, twexp GMM2 centers on a square-padded array and twgravity centers by the observed sum divided by n2n^2. The different centers change valid-cell regressors by a common shift, scaling the equation and its projection by a coefficient-dependent factor. At the root that factor cancels from the sandwich because the corresponding Jacobian term proportional to the moment is zero. A fully padded row or column contributes zero to both rectangular outcome products. In the directed calculation the diagonal is masked in both factors, so only rectangles made from observed links contribute.

The implementation contracts matrix products and sums without listing rectangles. In float64 it places a conservative bound of 150 on the absolute centered fitted index and on the log range of positive outcomes after common normalization. Ill-resolved cancellation, failed root checks and unusable covariance can lead to refusal. Function index

Predict trade after fitting

fit.predict() recovers origin and destination effects by PPML with the GMM slopes held fixed. The fitted trade totals match the observed origin and destination totals. Each residual is observed trade minus fitted trade.

For the directed fit above, the following compares fitted trade with trade predicted if every retained pair had a common language.

retained = bilateral_trade.iloc[fit.sample.positions]
fitted = fit.predict()
effects = fit.predict(type="fixed_effects")
residuals = fit.predict(type="residual")
same_language = fit.predict(retained.assign(common_language=1))

The second prediction uses the same slopes and recovered effects. See the runnable GMM example for synthetic data and prediction and counterfactuals for the retained-row requirements.

Correct coefficient bias from estimated effects

With many firms and a fixed number of years, cancelling firms can leave a fixed number of year effects. In gravity, the number of exporter-year and importer-year effects grows with the number of countries, even after cancelling pairs. Their estimation can shift the distribution of the slope by an amount comparable to its standard error. The growing-dimension result of Benatia et al. (2026) describes a leading bias of order d/nd/n when the number of retained coefficients dd is at most of order n\sqrt n under its information and moment conditions. A coefficient correction estimates and subtracts that leading bias. It is an explicit analysis choice. Benatia et al. (2026), §5.2, Theorem 2 and Appendix C.2

Correction after cancelling independent short groups

Use bias_correction="short_group" when the cancelled histories are the independent sampling units under the conditions of Benatia et al. (2026). The calculation uses their scores and derivatives at the uncorrected solution. It accounts for the association between each history’s score and derivative and for the curvature of the total score. In the fixed-year firm example the retained dimension is fixed, so a leading bias correction is unnecessary for a centered first-order limit. This call illustrates how to request it and report the change.

corrected = pm.fit(
    firm_formula, firms, cancel="firm", bias_correction="short_group", **common
)
print(corrected.summary())
powermean
====================================================================================
GPML (omega = 1, tau = 2)
Fixed effects: firm (cancelled), year (estimated)
Observations: 384 of 384 input rows (none dropped)
Status: verified; certified: True
Coverage: unique_root (BBP prop:fe-fixed-design)
BBP-corrected reported coefficients; certificate and first-order inference at the uncorrected estimating root.
   uncorrected      bias  estimate
0    -0.311998 -0.001029  -0.31097
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    coef.   std. err.        z    P>|z|    [95% conf. interval]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
price_index       -0.3110      0.0428    -7.27    0.000     -0.3948     -0.2272
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The reported coefficient is the uncorrected coefficient minus estimated bias. The standard error here is the first-order firm sandwich evaluated at the uncorrected root. In the covered growing-dimension gravity argument, Benatia et al. (2026) assume independent pair histories and dense support, such as complete off-diagonal pairs. A working variance other than PPML requires its own cancelled equation and the corresponding conditional moment.

The separate "cell" option uses the cell form of the correction. Its feasible cancelled version additionally needs growing cancellation groups to recover scales uniformly and the stated dependence and information conditions. A short-pair panel does not gain that justification from software acceptance. Powermean supplies these coefficient corrections on cancelled fits. Benatia et al. (2026), equations (5.5)–(5.7), the three-way panel remark and Appendix C.2

WZ for three-way PPML gravity

Weidner and Zylkin (2021) show that three-way PPML is consistent with a fixed number of years under their assumptions. Estimating exporter-year and importer-year effects can still shift the slope distribution and distort pair-clustered standard errors. The published analytical slope and covariance adjustments target those two sources of error.

Martin Weidner and Thomas Zylkin (2021). Bias and consistency in three-way gravity models. Journal of International Economics 132, 103513. The coefficient correction follows §3.4.2 and the expansion in Proposition 3. Published paper

Continue with trade and formula from the gravity walkthrough. Here the explicit covariance request keeps the ordinary pair sandwich while you inspect the coefficient adjustment.

wz_slope = pm.fit(
    formula,
    trade,
    omega=1,
    tau=1,
    cancel=None,
    bias_correction="wz",
    vcov={"cluster": "pair", "adjustment": "none"},
)
print(wz_slope.summary())
powermean

  importer^year: levels=96, redundant=8 (exact), nested in=none
Nested blocks count as fully redundant in these block counts.

For this draw the slope rises by about 0.004. tidy(), intervals and coefficient contrasts use the corrected point, with the requested covariance evaluated at the original root. After a WZ correction, fixef() and joint in-sample predictions remain at that root, as their metadata indicate. The correction works on unweighted built-in PPML with the three specified blocks, observed bread and the covered sample and normalization. See the exact WZ requirements before using it on a different panel.

Covariance refinements runs the separate WZ covariance request. These adjustments address leading terms under their respective assumptions. The single draw above illustrates the output.

Adjust pair covariance in three-way PPML

Ordinary pair clustering allows dependence within each pair’s history. In three-way PPML, estimating many country-year effects also changes the variability of the fitted scores used in that sandwich. The analytical adjustment of Weidner and Zylkin (2021) addresses this source of covariance bias. The coefficient correction is a separate calculation.

Martin Weidner and Thomas Zylkin (2021). Bias and consistency in three-way gravity models. Journal of International Economics 132, 103513. The pair-clustered covariance adjustment follows §3.4.3. Published paper

Change the covariance in the gravity example

Start with the uncorrected fit from the gravity walkthrough and the optional wz_slope from the coefficient chapter. The calls below use the retained fits, so the estimating equation is solved only once for each fit above. The same vcov mapping can be passed at fit time.

pair_wz = {"cluster": "pair", "adjustment": "wz"}
covariance_only = fit.with_vcov(pair_wz)
both_adjustments = wz_slope.with_vcov(pair_wz)

comparison = pm.etable(
    fit, covariance_only, both_adjustments,
    names=("Ordinary", "WZ covariance", "WZ coefficient and covariance"),
    scale="effect", uncertainty="ci", stars=False, digits=1,
)
print(comparison)

The ordinary and covariance-only columns report the same agreement effect. The WZ covariance adjustment widens the interval in this draw. The third column also applies the coefficient adjustment. Fitting with bias_correction="wz" and no covariance request selects the WZ pair adjustment by default. Use an explicit pair request to record which calculation you intend.

Plot the fitted effects and intervals

Use Matplotlib to draw the percentages and interval endpoints returned by effects(). That method reports proportions, so multiply the columns by 100 for the figure.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

effects = pd.concat([
    result.effects(["agreement"])
    for result in (fit, covariance_only, both_adjustments)
], ignore_index=True)
points = 100 * effects["estimate"]
lower = 100 * effects["conf_low"]
upper = 100 * effects["conf_high"]
labels = ["Ordinary", "WZ covariance", "WZ coefficient\nand covariance"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 2.8), layout="constrained")
ax.errorbar(points, labels, xerr=[points - lower, upper - points],
            fmt="o", color="#215873", capsize=4)
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set(xlabel="Change in expected trade (%)", title="Agreement effect with 95% intervals")
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.25)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.savefig("gravity-intervals.png", dpi=175)

Check the design before requesting WZ

The correction requires unweighted built-in PPML with directed pair, exporter-by-date and importer-by-date effects. Exporters and importers must come from the same set of at least three countries, with at least two dates and one record per observed date for every retained pair. Entire pairs can be absent, including diagonal pairs. A joint fit must keep the original unconditioned sample for the coefficient correction. A cancelled fit on this route must cancel the pair block. Pair independence, identifying variation and regularity conditions are part of the statistical argument. The callable domain for panel support is a software rule. Its acceptance on a given network does not establish a large-sample result for that network. Advanced FE options

Delete-group and higher-order covariance

The one-step delete-group covariance estimator of Benatia et al. (2026) combines approximations to changes in the target on omitting each independent short group. The higher-order result instead concerns covariance expectation bias after empirical coefficient correction. It requires additional smoothness, local solution and completion conditions. These two covariance estimators are outside the scope of Powermean. Benatia et al. (2026), Supplemental Appendix S3.4.2, Proposition S12, and S3.4.3, Proposition S13

Compare Powermean with ppmlhdfe

Use the gravity panel for a direct translation of the specification. Start by matching the rows and mean equation, then match the inference convention.

Match the gravity equation

fit = pm.fit(
    "trade ~ 0 + agreement | pair + exporter^year + importer^year",
    trade, omega=1, tau=1, cluster="pair",
)

With the same columns loaded in Stata, the corresponding syntax is

ppmlhdfe trade agreement, absorb(pair exporter#year importer#year) vce(cluster pair)

After | in Powermean, exporter^year names the exporter-year group, corresponding to the interaction in Stata’s absorb(). Cluster on the directed pair. In other designs, use offset="log_duration" or exposure="duration" to enter a known scale, when the formulation supports it. ppmlhdfe syntax

Check the sample and uncertainty

Check used rows, singleton and separated observations, excluded regressors, offsets and weights. The fixed-effect interface uses unit observation multipliers. Compare coefficients and fitted values at the same numerical accuracy. For uncertainty, also match the cluster classification, treatment of absorbed degrees of freedom, small-sample factor and reference distribution. Powermean conventions

Coefficient correction and WZ covariance adjustment are additional requests with their own domains. Use the same adjustment, or compare the uncorrected PPML fits. WZ options

When comparing elapsed time, include the same work in each timer. Capturing a formula and sample, solving, assessing the numerical point and computing uncertainty all take time. Compare first fits with first fits and prepared fits with prepared fits. Validation

Run the examples

Start with the 12-observation conditional-mean example to compare PPML, Gamma PML and an intermediate working variance.

Run the scripts from the source checkout or unpacked source distribution after installing Powermean. The datasets are generated locally from fixed seeds. The gravity and DiD chapters show the returned tables and include optional figure code using Matplotlib. To run the figure snippets, install Matplotlib in the same Python environment.

Example Script What to read
Gravity with zeros examples/first_fit.py Three-way PPML and coefficient bias corrections
Firm sales over four years examples/short_panel.py Firm-cancelled Gamma and counterfactual prediction
Nonlinear panel DiD examples/nonlinear_did.py Common and cohort-period effects
Two-way exponential regression examples/jochmans.py Fit GMM1 or GMM2 and predict for panels or directed pairs
No-FE PPML with IOLS docs/examples/iols_first_fit.py Check the IOLS installation

The sample comparison uses two fits of the same frame to show retained rows, exclusions, sample summaries and estimates. The prepared-fit example reuses a design across solvers, changes the covariance after estimation and reports a proportional contrast.

Reference and help

Function index

Examples use import powermean as pm. Choose the task you want to do.

Task Start here
Estimate a regression or reuse a design Fitting functions and supported methods by model.
Read an estimate, change its standard errors or test a restriction Result methods. GMM1 and GMM2 have a smaller set of result methods.
Predict outcomes, calculate residuals or recover fixed effects Prediction and fixed effects.
Find which rows were used or why a fit failed Sample and diagnostics and errors and warnings.
Describe data, compare fits or export a table Table functions and formats.
Simulate a panel or a dataset with a known slope Data generators and seed controls.

Fit and configure a model

pm.fit()

pm.fit(formula, data, **options) returns a Result for a power-mean regression or log OLS. Use the untransformed outcome on the left of the formula. Choose the conditional mean with omega and the working variance with either tau or variance. A formula with fixed-effect blocks fits them jointly by default. Use cancel="block" to cancel one named block. Fit options · Gravity fit · Nonlinear DiD

Set estimator="gmm1" or "gmm2" to difference out exactly two fixed-effect blocks using the moments derived in Jochmans (2017). Use an intercept-free formula. The default fe_layout="rectangular" requires a complete crossing. Set fe_layout="directed" for complete ordered non-self links. The returned JochmansResult reports coefficient inference, sample identity and a local root certificate. Two-way difference options · Method and example

pm.ppml()

pm.ppml(formula, data, **options) returns a PPML result with omega=1 and tau=1. With the gravity example’s formula and data, use pm.ppml(formula, trade, cluster="pair"). Gravity walkthrough · Working-variance comparison

pm.gpml()

pm.gpml(formula, data, **options) returns a Gamma PML result with omega=1 and tau=2. PPML and GPML require any explicit omega or tau to match their fixed values. Use pm.fit to supply a custom variance. Working-variance comparison · Short-panel example

pm.logols()

pm.logols(formula, data, **options) returns a least-squares result on the log outcome, with omega=0. Use positive_only=True to explicitly restrict data with zeros to the positive-outcome sample, then check fit.sample.positions. Exponentiating the fitted index gives the conditional geometric mean. Mean order and outcome domain · Worked log OLS call

pm.prepare()

pm.prepare(formula, data, **options) returns a Prepared object with the design and base inputs. Supply sample arguments and needed cluster classifications during preparation. prepared.positive_only records the fixed outcome-domain choice. prepared.fit(**options) returns a Result for that fit. Compare sample.positions when changing the mean order or equation. Sample arguments · Reuse a fit

pm.NB2()

pm.NB2(kappa=1.0) returns a working variance m + kappa*m**2. Pass variance=pm.NB2(kappa=0.5) in place of tau. The fit holds the finite, nonnegative kappa fixed. Read .kappa or call .to_dict() to inspect the choice. Given q = log(m), the variance object also provides log_value(q) for the log working variance, elasticity(q) for the derivative of log variance with respect to log mean, and elasticity_derivative(q) for its derivative with respect to q. Working variances

pm.ssc()

pm.ssc(*, robust, cluster, cluster_count, reference, psd, absorbed_count="fixest") returns an immutable convention to pass to a covariance request. The first five keywords are required. To save and restore the convention, use record.to_dict() and type(record).from_dict(record_dict). Small-sample conventions and example

pm.solver_defaults()

pm.solver_defaults(solver="newton") returns a SolverOptions record for Newton or an IolsOptions record for "iols". Use the fit’s solver= keyword to choose which solver runs. Solver options · IOLS options

newton_defaults = pm.solver_defaults().to_dict()
iols_defaults = pm.solver_defaults("iols").to_dict()

pm.SolverOptions()

pm.SolverOptions(max_iter=500) constructs a Newton options record with that iteration limit and the remaining defaults. Read its fields or call .to_dict(). Pass the record or a mapping as solver_options. Newton options and keyword defaults

See advanced fixed effects for optional module-level sample, solver and cancellation records.

Inspect a fitted result

The calls below apply to ordinary Result objects, including fixed effects estimated jointly or with one block cancelled. For the complete panel or dyad estimators, see GMM1 and GMM2 results.

Coefficients and uncertainty

coef()

fit.coef() returns a pandas Series of estimates indexed by term. Results

se()

fit.se() returns a Series of standard errors by term from the active covariance. Worked result

confint()

fit.confint(level=0.95) returns a DataFrame with lower and upper columns by term. Worked intervals

tidy()

fit.tidy(level=0.95) returns a coefficient DataFrame with estimates, standard errors, test statistics, p-values and interval endpoints. Worked coefficient table

summary()

fit.summary(level=0.95) returns a text report with estimates, sample counts and diagnostics. Use print(fit.summary()). Gravity report

Covariance and influence

vcov()

fit.vcov(spec=None, *, ssc=..., bread=...) returns a covariance DataFrame with metadata in .attrs. fit.vcov() reads the active covariance. An alternate spec requests a matrix at the fitted point, using retained information. Post-fit uncertainty · Worked covariance

with_vcov()

fit.with_vcov(spec, *, ssc=..., bread=...) returns a separate result view whose standard errors, intervals, tables, effects and tests use the requested covariance at the same fitted point. With fixed effects, supply only spec to either method. Put any supported ssc or bread override inside the request mapping. FE covariance options · Worked change of covariance

influence()

fit.influence(*, unit="sampling") returns a DataFrame of retained coefficient contributions, with a row per retained observation even under clustering. Cancellation gives one row per cancelled group by default. Use unit="row" for contributions indexed by original row position. Worked influence output

Effects and contrasts

These calls use the active covariance and report proportions with pointwise intervals. Choose ci="transform" for transformed endpoints or ci="delta" for a delta-method interval. Effects and tests

effect()

fit.effect(term, *, contrast=None, level=0.95, ci="transform") returns a proportional change record for one directly entered regressor. Supply contrast=(0, 1) for a zero-to-one change. Read estimate, std_error, interval, gradient or metadata. The record offers to_dict() and, with retained contributions, influence(). Agreement effect

effects()

fit.effects(terms=None, *, level=0.95, ci="transform") returns a DataFrame of one-unit changes for named direct regressors. With terms=None, it reports changes per coefficient coordinate. Cohort-by-date example

contrast()

fit.contrast(before, after, *, level=0.95, ci="transform") returns a proportional change record across two complete settings of the formula’s raw right-hand-side variables. It replays transformations and interactions while holding fixed effects and offsets fixed. Read the same estimate and interval fields as for effect(), or use to_dict(), to_frame() or influence() with retained contributions. Worked contrast

Coefficient combinations and restrictions

Use reported coefficient names in expressions. These calls use the active covariance. Both record types provide to_dict() and to_frame(). Worked combinations and tests

lincom()

fit.lincom(expression, *, level=0.95) returns an affine-combination record, for example from "x1 - x2". It includes estimate, std_error, interval, gradient, statistic, p_value and metadata. Worked linear combination

nlcom()

fit.nlcom(expression, *, level=0.95) returns the same kind of record for a smooth coefficient expression using arithmetic and exp. Use it for a coefficient-based change such as "exp(x1 - x2) - 1" with delta-method uncertainty. Worked nonlinear combination

test()

fit.test(expression) returns a restriction record for one affine equality such as "x1 = x2". Read its statistic, p_value and metadata. For a single restriction or a joint wald() test, difference contains the estimated restriction residuals and covariance their covariance matrix. Worked equality test

wald()

fit.wald(r, q) returns a restriction record for R beta = q. Supply a matrix with columns in fit.coef().index order and one entry of q per restriction row. Worked joint test

Predictions and fixed effects

predict()

fit.predict(data=None, *, type="power_mean") returns a Series of fitted conditional power means. Use type="fixed_effects" to extract the block Series returned by fixef(), or type="residual" for response residuals on the fit’s estimating scale. Both use the original fit sample. For fixed-effect counterfactuals, pass replacement covariates in the retained row order and keep the index. Slopes, offsets and fixed effects come from the fit. Fits without fixed effects also accept compatible new rows. Prediction · Worked prediction

fixef()

fit.fixef() returns a dictionary of block names to Series of normalized levels for an FE fit, including recovered levels for cancelled and two-way GMM fits. Fixed effects · Worked recovery

Sample and diagnostics

sample

fit.sample gives the input and retained counts (nobs, count), effective_n, zeros, counts, missing, and the row ledger. Use table() for exclusion counts and reason(position) for a specific row. The ledger includes zero-based positions, index labels, input_labels, retained_index and codes. Compare the retained positions before comparing estimates from fits on the same input frame, for example with with_price.sample.positions.tolist() == with_stock.sample.positions.tolist(). Sample · Worked row comparison

estimator

fit.estimator records the fitted equation, including mean order and working variance. Use fit.estimator.to_dict() for the resolved settings. Diagnostic records

certificate

fit.certificate gives the numerical assessment when the route produces one. Diagnostic records

provenance

fit.provenance gives the computation record, including the status, root-theory coverage label, options, trace and covariance where applicable. Use fit.provenance.to_dict() for export. Worked diagnostics

Build or export a table

All five functions return a Table. The four descriptive functions accept sample=fit with the original frame in its original row order, then apply their own missing-value rules. Summary and balance table options

pm.summary_statistics()

pm.summary_statistics(data, vars=None, **options) reports usable and missing counts, means, standard deviations and quantiles. For nonnegative variables it also reports zero shares and means among positive values. Compare retained samples

pm.balance_table()

pm.balance_table(data, treatment, vars=None, **options) reports covariate means by arm and differences from the selected control, with uncertainty and standardized differences. Baseline balance example

pm.balance_regression()

pm.balance_regression(data, treatment, vars=None, **options) regresses assignment on the covariates and reports coefficients and a joint test in a table. It compares each noncontrol arm with the control. Use continuous=True to regress the dose itself on the covariates. Baseline joint test

pm.outcome_table()

pm.outcome_table(data, outcomes, treatment, **options) reports outcome means, zero shares and unadjusted proportional comparisons by arm and mean order. Use the fitted result’s effect() or contrast() for an adjusted conditional change. Outcome table by promotion

pm.etable()

pm.etable(*results, **options) displays one model per column and reports the estimator, fixed effects, estimation sample and covariance choices. You can also pass one list or tuple of results. Use uncertainty="ci" to display intervals and scale="effect" to display percentage changes for coefficient coordinates. For a change involving several coefficients, use fit.contrast() for two regressor settings or fit.nlcom() for a coefficient expression. Regression tables · Worked model comparison

Table exports

Use table.to_frame(*, formatted=False) for a DataFrame with unrounded values or set formatted=True for the displayed cells. print(table) displays table.to_text(). For reports, use table.to_markdown(), table.to_html(), or table.to_latex(*, booktabs=True, floating=True, label=None). Export formats · Worked exports

Catch a refusal or inspect a warning

Inspect identifier, fields and message on the exception or warning. Existence and convergence errors also carry status, certificate and last_state when available. Troubleshooting

Public exception When to check it
pm.SpecificationError Invalid, conflicting or unsupported request.
pm.SampleError Invalid outcomes or no usable estimation rows.
pm.IdentificationError The remaining design fails to identify the parameters.
pm.ExistenceError The equation has no finite solution.
pm.SolverCapabilityError The solver does not support the requested case.
pm.ConvergenceError The solver failed to reach a reportable point.
Public warning What it describes
pm.CoverageWarning A limit of the available theory or a recognized change to the formula’s interpretation.
pm.NumericalWarning A numerical condition or assessment. Read status and certificate.
pm.CovarianceWarning A covariance adjustment or unavailable uncertainty.

Generate synthetic data

Import these names from powermean.testing. The four generators return Synthetic records. Their zeros option adds zeros in the simulation by randomly zeroing outcomes and rescaling the remaining values to preserve the conditional mean. Record the seed and draw to identify a dataset. Simulation validation

solver_data()

solver_data(design, *, n=1000, k=10, zeros=0.0, seed=SOLVER_SEED, draw=0, split="test") draws a no-FE dataset from SOLVER_DESIGNS with default seed SOLVER_SEED. Choose "development", "validation" or "test" for the seed split.

twoway_data()

twoway_data(design, *, n=2000, k=9, zeros=0.0, seed=TWOWAY_SEED, draw=0, split=40) draws a two-way FE dataset from TWOWAY_DESIGNS with default seed TWOWAY_SEED. The seed split is an integer.

threeway_data()

threeway_data(design, *, countries=20, years=5, zeros=0.0, seed=THREEWAY_SEED, draw=0, master=(100, 10), self_pairs=True) draws a directed dyadic panel from THREEWAY_DESIGNS with default seed THREEWAY_SEED. master gives the countries and periods of the underlying draw. Use self_pairs=False to exclude within-country pairs.

from powermean.testing import solver_data, threeway_data, twoway_data

no_fe = solver_data("G_poisson", draw=1, split="test")
two_way = twoway_data("d12", draw=1, split=40)
three_way = threeway_data("wz2", countries=8, years=3, draw=1)
metadata = three_way.metadata()

showcase_data()

showcase_data(*, law="nb2", regions=40, firms_per_region=5, years=6, zeros=0.0, seed=1, draw=0) draws a firm-year panel. Choose a law in SHOWCASE_LAWS for y and y_iv. SHOWCASE_TRUTH records the showcase coefficient values.

from powermean.testing import showcase_data

demo = showcase_data(regions=2, firms_per_region=2, years=3, seed=7)
print(demo.design, len(demo.frame))
print(demo.formula)
showcase/nb2 12
y ~ treat + x_normal + x_skewed + x_binary + C(category) + dose + C(arm) + policy | firm + year

showcase_treat_coefficient()

showcase_treat_coefficient(omega) returns the true coefficient of treat for the conditional power mean of the positive outcome y_pos at the requested order.

Synthetic

The dataset record contains design, frame, formula, truth, columns, seed, source, fingerprint and notes. Read zero_share for the fraction of zeros in y, digest() for numeric checks and metadata() for the JSON-compatible recipe and digest.

save()

save(data, path) takes a Synthetic record and a pathlib.Path ending in .csv or .dta. It writes the dataset and a companion JSON file with the same stem, and returns None.

Supported methods

Start with the mean you want to estimate. The formula, the treatment of fixed effects and the sampling design determine which estimators and standard errors you can use together.

Choose the model

Your data and question What to fit
Nonnegative outcome, including zeros Use pm.fit at a positive mean order. At omega=1, PPML (tau=1), Gamma PML (tau=2) and NB2 (variance=pm.NB2(kappa)) all model the arithmetic mean. Mean order and working variance
Outcome is strictly positive You can also model the geometric mean by log OLS (omega=0) or use a negative mean order. positive_only=True restricts the population represented by a fit when the original data include zeros. Outcome domain
Repeated observations with group differences Put one or more fixed-effect blocks after the formula’s vertical bar. The default fits them jointly. At a nonzero mean order, cancel="firm" cancels one named block while estimating the other blocks. Joint fixed effects · Cancellation in a short panel
Complete rectangular panel or directed array with two fixed-effect blocks GMM1 and GMM2 difference out both blocks under an additional assumption on products of errors across cells. Assumptions, eligible arrays and examples
Trade panel or policy adoption Fit three-way gravity or nonlinear difference-in-differences with pm.fit. The DiD example covers common and staggered adoption, cohort-by-period estimates and aggregation. Gravity · Nonlinear DiD

Set up the sample and estimation

  • Specify regressors and interactions in the formula. Use a subset to restrict rows, an offset or exposure for a known scale, and observation weights on supported fits without fixed effects. To reuse the same design, call pm.prepare and then prepared.fit. Data and formulas · Sample and weight options
  • Choose uncertainty to match the sampling design. Ordinary fits support robust, named HC, one-way or multiway cluster covariance within the relevant model’s scope. GMM1 and GMM2 use cell projections. Covariance and conventions · Fixed-effect covariance defaults
  • Newton is the default for nonlinear models. IOLS is available for certain positive-order models without fixed effects. Log OLS uses a linear solve. Outside the working-variance range 1 <= tau <= 2, a joint power-score fit at nonzero order seeks a local root. Read the numerical assessment before reporting it. Solver choices · Solver controls · IOLS installation
  • Coefficient bias corrections target distinct panel designs. Benatia et al. (2026) give the short-group and cell corrections for supported cancelled models. Weidner and Zylkin (2021) give a coefficient correction and a separate pair-covariance adjustment for three-way PPML. Coefficient bias · Covariance adjustment · Fixed-effect controls

Use the fitted model

Task Where to look
Check which observations entered or why a solve stopped Compare estimation samples · Diagnose unsuccessful fits
Calculate a percentage change, compare scenarios or test coefficients Proportional effects · Contrasts and tests
Predict outcomes, get residuals or extract group effects Prediction and counterfactuals · GMM1 and GMM2 results
Describe outcomes, check covariate balance or export a regression table Descriptive, balance and model tables
Generate synthetic data or find an exact call Simulation designs · Function index

Current scope limits

Powermean accepts a user-specified working variance. Automatic working-variance targeting, instrumental-variable estimation, HAC and Conley covariance, and the deletion and higher-order covariance estimators of Benatia et al. (2026) are unavailable. Reserved arguments · Papers and methods

Options

Use this page to translate a statistical choice into an exact argument. Start with the function that matches the mean and estimating equation, supply the sample decisions, then choose uncertainty and numerical controls. The walkthrough shows those choices in a complete analysis.

Fitting and preparation take a formula, a pandas DataFrame and named keywords. Unknown or conflicting requests raise SpecificationError. For reproducible results, record the installed version and the wheel or source archive used. Function index

Function Purpose
fit(formula, data, **options) Choose mean order and working variance, or select a two-way difference estimator.
ppml(formula, data, **options) Fix omega=1, tau=1.
gpml(formula, data, **options) Fix omega=1, tau=2.
logols(formula, data, **options) Fix omega=0; require positive outcomes.
prepare(formula, data, **options) Capture a problem for subsequent prepared.fit() calls.
solver_defaults(solver="newton") Inspect typed defaults: SolverOptions for Newton, the IOLS record for "iols".
NB2(kappa=1.0) Working variance m + kappa * m**2 with a fixed, finite kappa >= 0.
ssc(*, robust, cluster, cluster_count, reference, psd, absorbed_count="fixest") Declare a custom small-sample convention. The first five keywords are required. The record supports to_dict() and type(record).from_dict(...). See conventions.

Sample arguments

These arguments determine which observations and known scales enter the equation. They belong to preparation when you use a prepared problem.

Argument Default Meaning
positive_only False Explicitly restrict to positive outcomes.
weights Omitted Name of the weight column.
weight_type "analytic" With weights, choose "analytic" or "probability" to weight each row’s contribution, or "frequency" for integer replication counts. sample.effective_n sums the frequency counts.
offset Omitted A column or numeric expression on the log power mean scale.
exposure Omitted A positive column or expression whose logarithm is the offset.
subset Omitted Boolean condition per row, such as data["x"] > 0; missing conditions exclude rows.
retain Omitted For joint or cancelled fixed effects, name a column or sequence of columns to keep for later inference, such as retain="region" if you plan to call fit.vcov({"cluster": "region"}).

Use either offset or exposure. For repeated fits, supply these and the other sample arguments to pm.prepare(). prepared.positive_only records the outcome domain shared by its fits. Observation weights are available with Newton and log OLS when the formula has no fixed-effect blocks. For models with fixed effects or for IOLS, omit weights and weight_type. Prepare the data and formula

Fit and inference arguments

Once the sample is set, choose the mean order and working variance. The covariance describes sampling uncertainty; the solver controls how the equation is computed.

Argument Default Meaning
omega 1 Any finite real mean order; nonpositive orders require positive outcomes.
tau 1, or 2 for a cancelled pm.fit User-specified power variance index. Any finite value with Newton at a nonzero omega; outside [1, 2] the estimate is a selected root. IOLS and omega=0 accept [1, 2] only; see the range note. Cannot accompany variance.
variance Omitted A variance object, including pm.NB2(kappa); NB2 is refused with IOLS.
vcov "robust" for no-FE fits; see FE defaults below "robust"; a named HC method, "HC0" to "HC5" or "HC4m", never beside a cluster; or a cluster mapping: {"cluster": "unit"} for one classification, {"cluster": "a + b"} for several dimensions, with optional "multiway" and "psd" keys.
cluster Omitted Cluster shorthand; must agree with vcov if both appear.
ssc Omitted The covariance convention, given as "stata", "none", "regression" or a pm.ssc(...) record. If omitted, the default "stata" or the prepared request’s own convention applies. At fit time, pass ssc as a keyword alongside vcov or cluster.
bread "observed" Without fixed effects, "expected" is accepted only beside a named HC method; robust and cluster requests use the observed bread.
solver "newton" "newton", or the optional no-FE "iols"; order zero uses a dedicated linear calculation and refuses IOLS.
solver_options Canonical defaults A mapping or SolverOptions record; inspect pm.solver_defaults(). With IOLS, a mapping or the record from pm.solver_defaults("iols"). A no-FE Newton fit with tau outside [1, 2] also reads the root-Newton keys of the range note.
tol Canonical default Shorthand for the numerical tol; contradictory explicit values are refused.
start Automatic One finite value per retained coefficient on the reported scale; omit entries for dropped regressors. Refused with IOLS.
on_failure "raise" "return" permits inspection with inference withheld.
keep_influence True Retain contributions needed for subsequent requests.

Prepared fits use only clustering information retained during preparation. Convenience wrappers refuse contradictory mean or variance choices. The full numerical defaults and domains are in solver options, including the IOLS options.

Two-way difference options

Select estimator="gmm1" or "gmm2" in pm.fit and use an intercept-free formula with exactly two fixed-effect identifiers. These fits accept the following options and require the input to contain every cell of the chosen geometry. Filter the data frame first to fit on a smaller complete array. Two-way difference method

Argument Default Meaning
estimator Required for this route "gmm1" or "gmm2" selects the moment equation from Jochmans (2017), §III. Published paper
fe_layout "rectangular" A complete crossing of two dimensions, or "directed" for all ordered non-self links among common agents.
vcov "paper" Observed-cell normalization, or "stata" to match the directed Stata normalization.
start Zero slopes Finite starting slopes in formula design order.
max_iter 100 Maximum number of accepted Newton updates.

Full-family scope and the current entry restriction

The power-score family is not limited to the PPML-to-GPML interval. With Newton at a nonzero omega, an ordinary no-FE fit and a joint fit in the fixed-effect options accept any finite tau. Inside [1, 2] their convex Newton route is unchanged. Outside it, the estimate is a selected root of the specified equation. Unless start is supplied, root Newton starts from the certified fit of the nearest convex member on the same sample, at the requested mean order: tau=1 for tau < 1, tau=2 for tau > 2 (PPML and GPML at omega=1). If that fit is not certified, no root step runs and the result is not certified. A supplied start is used as given and recorded; it is not certified first, and no continuation path leaves from it. The certificate establishes a regular root; the root is not claimed to be unique or global.

Existence of a finite root is not characterized for tau < 1, or for tau > 2 with zero outcomes. Such a fit issues a CoverageWarning, drops no row for it and leaves the decision to the solver and the certificate. A wider family does not guarantee a finite root, identification or a certified fit for every user-specified value.

A no-FE fit outside [1, 2] reads six root-Newton keys from the same solver_options mapping: root_armijo, root_max_backtracks, root_max_iter, merit_metric ("gamma" or "gram"), continuation ("fallback" or "never") and continuation_step, as in solver_options={"merit_metric": "gram"}. Omitted keys, or a SolverOptions record, keep their defaults; other fits refuse these keys as unknown. A joint fit takes them in its nested root_options record instead; see advanced FE options. The resolved root options are recorded with the fit’s other numerical settings.

IOLS still accepts only [1, 2], and order zero still refuses powers outside that interval. Cancellation resolves any finite tau, or an NB2 variance, through its own routes and starts; the nearest convex start above applies to the no-FE and joint FE routes only.

Small-sample conventions

Use ssc to choose the convention for a robust, cluster or named HC request. Pass a preset ("stata", "none" or "regression") or an immutable record from pm.ssc. All six parameters are keyword-only. The first five are required. A value outside the table raises SpecificationError. The convention takes effect when a covariance request uses it.

Keyword Accepted values Role
robust "none", "N/(N-1)", "N/(N-K*)" Factor of a robust request.
cluster "none", "G/(G-1)", "(N-1)/(N-K*)*G/(G-1)" Factor of a cluster request.
cluster_count "min", "each" One factor with the smallest cluster count of a multiway request, or each component with its own count.
reference "normal", "t" Reference distribution of statistics, p-values and intervals.
psd "cgm", "fixest", "none" Treatment of an indefinite signed multiway estimate: reghdfe’s and ppmlhdfe’s eigenvalue adjustment in standardized coordinates, fixest’s rule (eigenvalues below 1e-12 set to 1e-12 on the reported matrix), or none.
absorbed_count "fixest" (default), "exact" Count of absorbed effects for fixed-effect log OLS when the covariance factor or reference uses that count.

Here K* is the count K_factor used by the factor. With fixed effects it is the number of retained regressors plus the count of the absorbed parameters. For fixed-effect log OLS (omega=0), "fixest" counts levels less one per counted block after the first. "exact" uses the rank of the counted indicators. For clustered log OLS, both rules exclude blocks nested in a requested cluster dimension and subtract one from the count if any block is nested and any counted block remains. HC1 uses the chosen count for its factor. The default robust convention uses N/(N-1) and a normal reference. Other joint fits use the indicator rank with the cluster nesting adjustment. Only fixed-effect log OLS supports absorbed_count="exact" among FE fits. For the named HC methods of cancelled fits, redundant levels are removed exactly for one and two blocks and by a pairwise bound, taken in the order of the formula, from the third block on. Covariance metadata

A robust or cluster request applies its convention’s factor once and uses its reference. A signed multiway request without its own "psd" key also uses its psd treatment. A named HC method keeps its own factor and takes the convention’s reference. An omitted or inherited convention never adds its factor to that method. An explicit convention with robust factor "none" adds nothing; an explicit factor identical to the method’s own, by formula and exact counts, is that same correction applied once. Any other explicit factor is refused as a second correction. For robust or cluster requests, an explicit "stata" keeps the default factors and is recorded as requested.

For a robust fit without fixed effects, use the data frame from the worked no-FE example.

import powermean as pm

convention = pm.ssc(
    robust="N/(N-1)",
    cluster="G/(G-1)",
    cluster_count="min",
    reference="normal",
    psd="cgm",
)
fit = pm.fit("y ~ 1 + x1 + x2", data, vcov="robust", ssc=convention)

When a fit of a prepared problem gives vcov or cluster, that request and its convention replace the prepared ones; ssc given alone applies to the prepared request, as does bread to a prepared named HC method. After a fit without fixed effects, vcov(spec, ssc=...) and with_vcov(spec, ssc=...) use the request’s explicit convention or inherit the fit’s. Both reuse the fitted point. See the fixed-effect options for FE requests.

Fixed-effect options

Write the effect blocks after | in the formula. To cancel one block, name it with cancel="block", or use cancel=True to select the unique largest block. Ordinary fixed-effect calls use the package’s sample and solver defaults. Within solver_options, choose absorbed="index" to use the index organization instead of the default "profiled". Preparation remains order-neutral. Advanced FE options explains the optional control records and their supported domains.

FE fits use Newton; solver="iols" is refused. Through pm.fit, a cancelled call that omits both tau and variance uses power tau=2, not the ordinary default tau=1.

Fit-time covariance for fixed effects

For an ordinary joint fit with no covariance request, Powermean clusters on the pair if the three retained fixed-effect blocks identify a unique pair, origin-by-date and destination-by-date structure. For example, the pair block can be pair in pair + origin^year + destination^year, provided it groups the same endpoint pairs on the retained sample. If no such structure is established, the ordinary default remains "robust". If more than one assignment is valid, specify the intended cluster explicitly, for example cluster="pair" for a block named pair.

An explicit covariance request, including vcov="robust", takes precedence on this route. Omitting covariance does not request a coefficient correction or the WZ covariance adjustment. WZ-corrected fits and cancelled fits use their own covariance rules.

At fit time, joint fits accept robust, "HC0" to "HC5", "HC4m" and one-way or multiway cluster requests, subject to the requirements of each covariance. Supply ssc= and bread= as fit keywords. Cancelled fits also accept robust, named HC and one-way or multiway cluster requests within their domains. They use observed bread. FE fits also accept bias_correction (False, True, "short_group", "cell" or "wz") within the correction domains. Fixed-effect fits use unit multipliers. Supplied observation weights are unavailable. Unsupported families, domains and inference requests are refused; see the package API documentation and availability.

Post-fit covariance for fixed effects

Use fit.vcov() to read the active covariance. For a supported alternate request, fit.vcov(spec) returns a matrix and fit.with_vcov(spec) returns a result view. Both require an accepted fit and the information needed for the request. For clustering, the classifications must be available from the fit. Recompute uncertainty

FE results accept ssc and bread overrides as keys inside the request mapping, subject to the covariance’s domain. For example, with a joint FE fit and the convention above, use fit.vcov({"method": "robust", "ssc": convention}). Pass any overrides through spec for both methods.

Covariance adjustment key

Ordinary no-FE calls refuse the vcov mapping key adjustment. In FE requests, {"cluster": pair, "adjustment": "wz"} asks for Weidner and Zylkin’s three-way PPML covariance adjustment, at fit time or through vcov(spec), within its documented domain. Under bias_correction="wz", an explicit "adjustment": "none" keeps the ordinary pair-cluster covariance. The key does not activate either covariance refinement of Benatia et al. (2026). See covariance refinements for the statistical distinctions.

Deferred HAC and Conley requests

HAC and Conley covariance are unavailable. The reserved FE request forms below result in an unavailable or invalid request diagnostic.

Request Reserved mapping keys Typed record
HAC {"hac": time, "unit": unit, "lag": lag, "step": step} HacRequest(time, unit=..., lag=..., step=...)
Conley {"conley": [latitude, longitude], "cutoff": cutoff, "units": units, "distance": distance, "pool_times": True} ConleyRequest(latitude, longitude, cutoff=..., units=..., distance=..., pool_times=...)

The records are defined in powermean.data.inference_requests, not as root exports pm.HacRequest or pm.ConleyRequest. The variable names in the table stand for column names and explicit settings; optional fields may be omitted. None is a supplied value, not omission.

For HAC, time and an explicitly supplied unit are column names. lag is a nonnegative integer and step is a positive integer. Omitted lag represents the reserved automatic-lag request; the record’s omitted step represents one period. No lag rule, time grid validation or covariance calculation runs here.

For Conley, the two column names are latitude then longitude. cutoff is a finite nonnegative number, including zero. Explicit units is "km" or "mi" and requires an explicit cutoff. distance is "triangular" or "spherical". pool_times, when supplied, accepts only True. Reserved omission metadata represents kilometers and triangular distance, with an automatic cutoff request if cutoff is omitted. This does not validate coordinates or repeated locations, choose a numerical cutoff or compute a spatial covariance. It does not substitute another covariance or refit.

Reserved requests

Automatic working-variance selection (targeted IOLS) is unavailable. The tau and variance arguments choose a working variance you provide; neither requests automatic targeting, and solver="iols" computes the equation you specified.

The keywords advise, gmm and threads are reserved. Supplying any of them raises an unsupported-feature error. To fit GMM1 or GMM2, use the estimator option on a complete two-way array. Coefficient bias correction requires a supported fixed-effect fit. Instrumental-variable estimation is unavailable. For a model without fixed effects, expected bread is available with a named HC covariance.

Inactive cancel=None, difference=False, bias_correction=False and moment="multiplicative" are accepted, as is bread="observed" beside a robust or cluster request. Without fixed effects, ssc always belongs to the covariance request; see small-sample conventions. See availability.

For computational controls, continue to Solver options. For inspecting a returned fit, use Results.

Choose a solver and read its assessment

The mean model specifies the target and the working variance specifies the estimating equation. The solver computes a point satisfying that equation. For instance, the default solver in the gravity example computes joint PPML with three absorbed blocks.

Which calculation runs?

Nonlinear calls default to Newton. Joint and cancelled FE fits use their corresponding Newton procedures, with the profiled organization as the default. Order zero uses least squares on the log outcome. Keep solver settings separate from the order, working variance and cancellation choice.

For nonzero order and a power tau outside [1, 2], joint and no-FE calls compute a selected root. Unless you supply start, the procedure starts from a certified fit of the nearest convex family member on the same sample. The available root need not be unique, and some combinations have narrower existence results. Cancellation uses its own starting rules. If continuation runs, earlier certified stages supply starting values. The reported result and its certification always use the requested tau. Power-variance range

What the convergence assessment checks

The certificate assesses the computed point with diagnostics appropriate to the equation, which can include score residuals, index corrections and fixed-effect equations. Inspect the status if the achieved tolerance differs from the request. When the assessment fails, inference is withheld. Use on_failure="return" to inspect the returned state. Solver options · Troubleshooting

The exact-score completion of Benatia et al. (2026) returns to the original estimating equation after solving approximations. Under the conditions in its numerical argument, the remaining numerical error is negligible at the statistical scale. A numerical assessment at one sample shows how well that point solves the equation. Establishing a valid population interpretation requires the assumptions of the chosen model and estimator. Benatia et al. (2026), §4 and Supplemental Appendix S2

IOLS: an optional no-FE solver

Iterated ordinary least squares uses shifted-log approximations and repeated least-squares steps to compute a specified power-score equation. The shifts scale with the outcome and fitted mean. A fixed shift before one log regression solves a different problem. Powermean offers solver="iols" for no-FE fits with positive order, a power tau in [1, 2], an intercept, at least one other regressor and more observations than coefficients. The route excludes NB2, weights, offsets, exposure and a supplied start.

The prepared-fit example solves one equation by both Newton and IOLS. IOLS can use a compiled loop or a NumPy implementation. The result records the implementation. To inspect or request one, see IOLS installation and IOLS controls.

Solver options

Use solver controls after specifying the sample, model and estimating equation. They govern computational accuracy and effort. They do not change which population quantity the model targets or which observations can be dependent. Numerical methods explains the distinction.

The ordinary defaults below apply to Newton, the default solver. The optional IOLS solver has its own record, described after the Newton table. Inspect the installed version before changing a setting:

import powermean as pm

options = pm.solver_defaults()
print({key: options.to_dict()[key] for key in ("tol", "max_iter", "curvature")})
iols_options = pm.solver_defaults("iols")
print({key: iols_options.to_dict()[key] for key in ("iols_backend", "stopcrit")})
{'tol': 1e-08, 'max_iter': 100000, 'curvature': 'observed'}
{'iols_backend': 'cpp', 'stopcrit': 1000000}

Ordinary Newton options

Option Default Accepted values and role
tol 1e-8 Positive finite real; strict numerical threshold.
tol_secondary 1e-6 Positive finite real; secondary numerical threshold.
coef_tol 1e-6 Positive finite real; coefficient accuracy diagnostic threshold.
rcond_min 1e-13 Strictly between zero and one; conditioning safeguard.
newton_provider "bundled" "bundled" or compatible installed "sklearn".
gradient_tol 1e-10 Positive finite real; iteration gradient threshold.
max_iter 100000 Positive integer; iteration budget.
max_evaluations 1000000 Positive integer; evaluation budget.
armijo 2**-11 Strictly between zero and one; sufficient decrease setting.
backtrack_factor 0.5 Strictly between zero and one; step reduction factor.
max_backtracks 21 Positive integer; backtracking budget.
retry 1 Integer zero or one; the solver’s specified retry control.
curvature "observed" "observed" or "expected" for the Newton system.

The solver’s curvature option is not the inference argument bread. Expected curvature in an iteration does not activate expected bread covariance. retry=1 allows at most one retry. In an eligible profiled fixed-effect fit, if the first attempt fails to find a numerical step, complete its line search or finish the inner absorption, the solver may restart from the original coefficient start, opening with all the fixed effects estimated together. The retry uses the remaining budgets and the same sample and accuracy requirements. If it does not certify, the original refusal stands. Set retry=0 to disable retries.

Pass a mapping through solver_options or a complete SolverOptions record. Unknown keys are errors. Booleans are not numeric tolerances or budgets; a floating point value is not accepted in place of an integer budget.

The top level tol keyword is shorthand for the nested tol. If both are explicit, they must agree exactly. A complete SolverOptions record counts as explicit values, including the fields equal to defaults.

IOLS options

solver="iols" selects IOLS for a supported no-FE fit. Its solver_options is a mapping or the record returned by pm.solver_defaults("iols"), not a SolverOptions record. In a mapping, tol, tol_secondary, coef_tol and rcond_min keep the certificate roles, domains and defaults of the table above, and the top level tol follows the same agreement rule.
